posts.topic: Giving as a business strategy
posts.hook: Giving isn't the cost of doing business. It's the business.
posts.caption:
Giving isn't the cost of doing business. It's the business.

Early in my career, someone told me that charity work was "nice, but it won't pay the bills."

Twenty-plus years, more than 2,500 events and over $70 million raised for charity later, I can tell you they were wrong. Not a little bit wrong. Completely wrong.

Giving has paid my bills. It has built my reputation, opened doors I couldn't have knocked down on my own, and introduced me to almost every person who matters in my professional life.

But here's the part people miss: it only works if you're not doing it for the return.

The moment giving becomes a transaction, people can smell it. The cheque handed over for the photo. The sponsorship that disappears when the cameras leave. The "partnership" that's really just a logo on a banner.

Real giving as a strategy looks different. It looks like:

Turning up to the charity committee meeting on a wet Tuesday night when nobody's watching.

Giving your expertise, not just your money. My skill is events, so that's what I give.

Staying for years, not for a campaign.

Asking "what do you actually need?" instead of "what can I sponsor?"

What comes back isn't immediate, and it isn't predictable. It's trust. And trust compounds.

The CEO you sat next to at a fundraiser five years ago remembers that you stayed to stack chairs. The board member you supported quietly becomes the person who recommends you for the contract you didn't even know existed.

I've never once sat down and written "giving" into a business plan as a lead-generation tactic. But if I'm honest, it has been the single most powerful growth strategy I've ever had.

I kept giving and kept showing up, without knowing where it would lead.

If you're wondering where to start, think about a skill you have that a cause you care about could use.

Start with that skill.

What's the cause closest to your heart, and what could you give it that money can't buy?

#Philanthropy #PurposeDrivenBusiness #WomenInBusiness #CharityEvents #Leadership

posts.topic: Networking in earnest
posts.hook: I stopped "networking" years ago. My network has never been stronger.
posts.caption:
I stopped "networking" years ago. My network has never been stronger.

I need to confess something: I've never loved the word networking.

It conjures up name tags, lukewarm wine, and people scanning the room over your shoulder for someone more useful to talk to. Business cards pushed into your hand before you've even said your name.

We've all been on the receiving end of that. And if we're honest, most of us have probably done it too.

At some point in my career, I made a decision. I would stop networking and start meeting people in earnest.

Here's what that looks like for me:

I go to fewer events, and I stay longer. I'd rather have three real conversations than thirty handshakes.

I ask questions I actually want the answer to. Not "what do you do?" but "what are you working on that you're excited about?" or "what's been the hardest part of your year?"

I don't lead with what I sell. If there's a fit, it will come up naturally. If there isn't, I've still met an interesting person.

I look for the person standing on their own. Some of the most valuable relationships of my career started with someone who looked uncomfortable at the edge of the room.

I follow up with something useful: an introduction, an article or a simple message saying, "That thing you mentioned? I know someone who might be able to help."

The result? My network today isn't wide. It's deep. These are people who pick up when I call. People I'd drop everything for, and who'd do the same for me.

And yes, it has been incredibly good for business. But that's the by-product, not the point.

Networking in earnest is slower. It takes more energy. It requires you to be genuinely interested in other humans.

But it's the only kind that lasts.

What's the best question someone has ever asked you at a networking event? The one that made you feel truly seen?

#Networking #Relationships #WomenInBusiness #Connection #BusinessGrowth

posts.topic: Questions to ask your keynote speakers
posts.hook: The keynote speaker questions most event organisers forget to ask
posts.caption:
The keynote speaker questions most event organisers forget to ask

A great keynote can make an event. A mismatched one can sink it.

In more than two decades of producing conferences, galas and corporate events, I've seen both. Brilliant speakers who left a room buzzing for weeks. And big names who delivered a generic talk they'd clearly given a hundred times, to an audience they knew nothing about.

The difference almost always comes down to the questions asked before the booking.

Here are the ones I never skip:

1. "Who is this talk really for?" Ask the speaker to describe the audience their keynote works best with. If it isn't your audience, keep looking, however impressive the name.

2. "How will you tailor this to our event?" A great speaker will want to know your theme, your audience's challenges and your goals. If they don't ask you questions back, that's a red flag.

3. "Can I see unedited footage of you speaking?" Highlight reels are beautifully edited. I want to see 10 minutes of the real thing, warts and all.

4. "What do you want the audience to think, feel and do differently afterwards?" If they can't answer this clearly, the talk probably won't land clearly either.

5. "How long is the talk, and how strictly do you keep to time?" One speaker running 20 minutes over can throw out an entire day.

6. "What do you need from us technically?" Confirm slides, clicker, microphone, confidence monitor and video playback early.

7. "Will you stay for the event?" Speakers who join the networking, sit in on other sessions and mingle at lunch add enormous value. Speakers who arrive, speak and leave feel like a booking, not a guest.

The right speaker isn't the most famous one you can afford. It's the one who connects most deeply with the people in your room.

Event organisers, what's the one question you always ask a keynote speaker? Let's build a useful list together.

#EventPlanning #KeynoteSpeaker #Conferences #EventProfs #EventProduction

posts.topic: Giving being part of the DNA
posts.hook: You can't bolt generosity onto a business. It has to be in the bones.
posts.caption:
You can't bolt generosity onto a business. It has to be in the bones.

I've watched plenty of companies try to add giving the way you'd add a new product line.

A CSR policy gets written. A charity partner gets chosen by committee. Someone in marketing is told to "post about it." And twelve months later, nobody can remember why they started.

That's because giving that sits on the outside of a business is always the first thing to go when times get tight.

Giving that sits inside the business, in the DNA, survives everything.

When I think about what that actually means, it comes down to a few things I've tried to build into every business I've led:

It shows up in the decisions nobody sees. Which suppliers you choose. Whether you pay small businesses on time. Whether you discount for a grassroots charity that can't afford full price, and never mention it publicly.

It's in how you hire. I look for people who light up when they talk about something bigger than themselves. You can teach someone to run a production schedule. It's much harder to teach them to care.

It's in the language. In my world, we don't say "charity clients." We say partners. Because we're in it together, and their mission becomes part of ours for the life of that event and long after.

It's modelled from the top. If the leader isn't giving their time, energy and presence, nobody else will believe it's real. My team has seen me on my hands and knees taping down cables at a gala at midnight. That matters more than any values poster on the wall.

Here's the thing about DNA: you don't have to remind it to work. It just does.

When giving is part of who you are, you don't need a campaign to prove it. Your clients feel it in every interaction. Your team feels it on a Monday morning. Your community feels it when you turn up year after year.

And when the hard seasons come, and they always do, it's the thing that holds you together.

So if you lead a team, ask yourself honestly: if you stopped talking about giving tomorrow, would anyone notice it was missing from what you do?

That's the real test.

What's one small, unseen habit that shows a business truly cares? I'd love to hear yours.

#Leadership #CompanyCulture #Philanthropy #PurposeDriven #WomenWhoLead

posts.topic: Why volunteering is so important
posts.hook: Volunteers are the invisible infrastructure of this country
posts.caption:
Volunteers are the invisible infrastructure of this country

Every large charity event I've ever produced has had one thing in common.

Behind the lighting rig, the stage, the auction and the beautifully set tables, there's an army of volunteers holding the whole thing together.

The people at registration at 5pm who've been there since noon. The students running auction paddles. The retirees folding programs. The corporate team who gave up a Saturday to pack 3,000 gift bags.

Without them, most of the $70 million I've helped raise simply wouldn't exist.

I don't think we talk enough about how much this country runs on volunteers. Sporting clubs. School canteens. Emergency services. Aged care visits. Food banks. Community festivals. This quiet, unpaid and often unthanked work holds our communities together.

And yet volunteering is getting harder. People are busier, more stretched, more tired. Many organisations I work with are struggling to find the hands they need.

Here's why I believe volunteering matters so much:

It fills gaps no budget can. Charities simply cannot afford to pay for every hour of work their mission requires.

It builds community in a lonely world. Some of the strongest friendships I've seen formed between people who'd never have met otherwise, side by side at a volunteer table.

It reminds us what we're capable of. There's something powerful about doing hard, useful work for no reward except knowing it mattered.

It creates the next generation of leaders. Many of the best event professionals I know started as volunteers.

You don't need to commit every weekend. One shift. One event a year. One skill offered to a cause you love.

If every business in Australia gave each of their staff one volunteer day a year, imagine what we could do.

When did you last volunteer, and what did it give you that you didn't expect?

#Volunteering #Community #CharitySector #GivingBack #Leadership

posts.topic: Questions to ask your MC before booking
posts.hook: Your MC can make or break your event. Ask these questions before you book.
posts.caption:
Your MC can make or break your event. Ask these questions before you book.

People spend months choosing the venue, the menu and the keynote speaker. Then they book the MC in a rush, two weeks out, because "someone knows someone who's good on a microphone."

After producing more than 2,500 events and stepping into the MC role myself, I know how much this choice matters.

They set the tone. They hold the timing. They manage the energy. They rescue you when things go wrong. And they're the voice your guests will associate with your entire event.

Here's what I ask every MC before I book them:

1. "What types of events do you MC most often?" Comedy nights, corporate conferences, charity galas and awards ceremonies all need different skills. You want someone experienced in your kind of room.

2. "How do you prepare?" Listen for: research into the organisation, a briefing call, studying the run sheet, learning name pronunciations. If the answer is "I just wing it," walk away.

3. "How do you handle a speaker running over time?" This tells you whether they'll protect your schedule or let it unravel.

4. "Tell me about a time something went wrong on stage." Every experienced MC has a story. How they tell it tells you how they'll handle your inevitable hiccup.

5. "How do you balance personality with professionalism?" You want warmth and humour, but the event isn't their stand-up set. The best MCs know when to step forward and when to step back.

6. "Can I see you in action?" Footage of a full segment, not just a highlight reel. Better still, a referee you can call.

A great MC helps the whole event feel effortless. Guests leave remembering a well-run day, even if they don't notice all the work that held it together.

What's the best (or worst) MC experience you've had at an event?

#EventPlanning #MC #EventProfs #Conferences #CharityEvents

posts.topic: Building The Giving Table
posts.hook: Why I built The Giving Table
posts.caption:
Why I built The Giving Table

After more than twenty years in business, I kept noticing the same gap.

There were plenty of networking groups, business clubs and charity committees. I wanted a place that brought those things together, where women could grow their businesses, build real friendships and make a difference at the same table.

So I built one.

The Giving Table is a purpose-driven community for women in business. We connect through networking, events and masterclasses. But the thing that makes it different is the word in the middle of the name.

Giving.

I've spent my career watching what happens when generosity sits at the centre of business. Doors open. Trust deepens. Opportunities appear that you could never have planned for. I wanted to create a space where that wasn't a happy accident, but the whole point.

Here's what I wanted The Giving Table to be:

A room where women don't have to perform. No hard sells. No posturing. Just real conversations with women who get it.

A place to learn from people who've actually done it. Our speakers and masterclass hosts are practitioners, not theorists.

A community that gives back together. Charity isn't an add-on. It's woven through everything we do.

A network that lasts. Not a monthly event you attend and forget, but relationships that carry you through the highs and lows of business.

Building it has been rewarding and humbling. It has asked me to practise everything I preach about generosity, consistency and showing up.

And watching women in our community win clients, launch businesses, find mentors and support causes together? That's the best return I could ask for.

If you've ever walked out of a networking event feeling more drained than inspired, I built this for you.

What would your ideal business community give you that you haven't found yet?

#TheGivingTable #WomenInBusiness #PurposeDriven #WomenSupportingWomen #Community

posts.topic: Networking in earnest
posts.hook: The networking mistake I see smart women make over and over
posts.caption:
The networking mistake I see smart women make over and over

I host and attend a lot of events for women in business. I see the same thing happen again and again.

Brilliant, accomplished women walk into a room and immediately shrink.

They hover near the people they already know. They apologise for interrupting. They describe their business in a way that undersells it by about 80 per cent. And they leave without asking for the one thing they came for.

I understand it, because I've done it. Early in my career, I'd walk into rooms full of senior men in suits and feel like I needed permission to be there.

Here's what I've learnt since, and what I now tell every woman who joins our community:

You are allowed to say what you want. If you're looking for a mentor, a partner, a client or an introduction, say so. People can't help you if they don't know what you need.

Lead with curiosity, not credentials. The most magnetic person in any room is the one who makes others feel interesting.

Know your one-line story. Not your job title. The thing you do and why it matters. Practise it until it rolls off your tongue without a hint of apology.

Bring someone in. When you see a woman on her own, bring her into your conversation. Generosity in a room is remembered long after the event.

Follow up within 48 hours. Momentum is everything. A warm connection goes cold surprisingly fast.

Remember it's a long game. You don't need to close anything tonight. You need to be remembered for the right reasons.

Networking in earnest isn't about being the loudest voice. It's about being the most genuine one.

The room needs what you bring. Don't hide it at the drinks table.

What's one thing you wish someone had told you before your first big networking event?

#WomenInBusiness #Networking #Confidence #WomenSupportingWomen #CareerGrowth

posts.topic: Charity support
posts.hook: What charities wish businesses knew (from someone who's sat in both chairs)
posts.caption:
What charities wish businesses knew (from someone who's sat in both chairs)

I've spent more than two decades working alongside charities. I've helped raise over $70 million. And I've had hundreds of honest, behind-closed-doors conversations with the people who run them.

Here's what they've told me and what most of them will never say out loud to a sponsor.

"Unrestricted funding changes everything." Everyone wants their money to buy the ambulance or fund the program with the nice photo. But charities also need to pay rent, keep the lights on and retain good staff. Money with no strings is the most valuable gift you can give.

"Please don't make us chase you." A charity's team is often tiny. Every hour they spend chasing a pledge, an invoice or a logo file is an hour not spent on the mission. Be easy to work with.

"We'd rather have you for five years than for one big event." Charities plan budgets years ahead. Consistency lets them hire, grow and make promises to the people they serve.

"Your expertise is worth as much as your money." Accountants, lawyers, marketers, event producers -  your skills can save a charity tens of thousands of dollars. Offer them.

"Come and see what we actually do." The businesses that visit, volunteer and meet the people behind the cause become the most committed partners. Every single time.

"Don't make it all about you." Recognition is fair. But when the sponsorship ask is mostly about logo placement and photo opportunities, it shows.

I say all of this with love, because I know most businesses genuinely want to help. They just haven't been told how.

The gap between what businesses offer and what charities need is one of the biggest missed opportunities I see. Close that gap, and the impact multiplies.

If you work in the charity sector, what would you add to this list? And if you're a business supporting a cause what's one thing you'd love charities to understand about you?

#CharitySector #NotForProfit #Philanthropy #CorporatePartnerships #Fundraising

posts.topic: Relationships over sporadic connections
posts.hook: The relationships behind the connection count
posts.caption:
The relationships behind the connection count

I have a lot of LinkedIn connections. I'm grateful for every one of them.

But if my business hit a crisis at midnight tonight, there are maybe a handful of people I could call who would pick up, listen, and roll up their sleeves.

Those people are the reason I'm still in business after twenty years.

We live in a time where connection has never been easier and relationship has never been rarer. One click, and you're "connected." One like, and you've "engaged." One coffee every two years, and you call it a relationship.

It isn't.

The relationships that have shaped my career have a few things in common:

They were built over years, not meetings. Many of my closest business relationships started with someone I barely spoke to for the first year.

They survived a disagreement. If you've never been honest with each other, you don't really know where you stand.

They include giving with no ledger. Nobody's keeping score.

They show up in the hard moments. The phone call when a contract falls over. The message when someone hears you're unwell. The person who turns up to your event when it rains and half the guest list doesn't.

Sporadic connections are fine. They're pleasant. Occasionally, they turn into something.

But if you want a business that can weather anything, you need to invest in depth over breadth.

That means choosing your people deliberately. Checking in when you don't need anything. Remembering birthdays, kids' names, the surgery they were nervous about. Celebrating their wins as loudly as your own.

It's slower. It's less scalable. It doesn't look impressive on a dashboard.

When a difficult moment comes, you learn which relationships you can rely on.

Who's one person in your professional life you could call at midnight? Maybe today's the day to tell them they matter.

#Relationships #Leadership #BusinessGrowth #Connection #Gratitude

posts.topic: Why volunteering is so important
posts.hook: To every business leader who thinks volunteer days are a "nice to have"
posts.caption:
To every business leader who thinks volunteer days are a "nice to have"

If your business doesn't offer volunteer leave, it's worth considering what it could bring to your team and your community.

I've watched it play out with corporate teams at countless charity events. A group arrives on a Saturday morning, slightly awkward, in matching t-shirts. By the end of the day, they're laughing, swapping stories and working together in a way that no team-building workshop could ever manufacture.

Here are some of the ways I've seen volunteering bring a team together:

It flattens the hierarchy. When the CFO and the graduate are both stacking chairs, something shifts. People see each other as humans first.

It gives people perspective. Spend a day at a food relief centre and your inbox doesn't feel quite so urgent on Monday.

It builds pride. People want to work for businesses that stand for something. Your best talent is watching what you do, not what you say.

It develops real skills. Problem-solving under pressure. Communication with people from different walks of life. Leadership without a title.

It can strengthen retention. When people feel connected to the purpose of their work, it gives them another reason to stay.

The objection I hear most is cost: "We can't afford to lose a day of productivity."

It deserves a practical conversation. Start with a level of time and support the business can sustain, then ask the team and charity what worked.

Start small if you need to. One team day a year. Partner with a charity that matches your values. Let your people choose the cause.

Then watch what happens to your culture.

If your workplace offers volunteer leave, what difference has it made? And if it doesn't, what's stopping you?

#CorporateVolunteering #CompanyCulture #EmployeeEngagement #CSR #Leadership

posts.topic: Building The Giving Table
posts.hook: What I've learnt building a community (that nobody tells you)
posts.caption:
What I've learnt building a community (that nobody tells you)

Building The Giving Table has taught me more than I expected. Some of it was joyful. Some of it kept me up at night.

Here's what I've learnt about building a real community, for anyone thinking of starting one:

1. Community is built in the in-between moments. The event is the easy part. The real community lives in the follow-up messages, the introductions made over coffee, the members checking in on each other between gatherings.

2. You have to model the culture you want. If I want members to be generous, I have to be generous with my time, my contacts and my honesty.

3. Not everyone is your person, and that's okay. A community with a clear purpose will naturally attract some people and not others. Trying to be everything to everyone dilutes the very thing that makes it special.

4. Structure creates freedom. Clear ways to take part help people find the level of involvement that suits their life and business.

5. Consistency matters. One extraordinary event won't build a community on its own. People need to know you'll keep showing up.

6. Listen more than you plan. Some of our best ideas have come straight from members telling me what they need.

7. It will stretch you. Building a community means holding space for other people's ambitions, struggles and growth while still managing your own. It's a privilege, and it's also a lot.

Would I do it again? In a heartbeat.

Watching a room full of women realise that someone has their back makes the effort worthwhile.

Have you ever been part of a community that truly changed your business or your life? What made it work?

#CommunityBuilding #TheGivingTable #WomenInBusiness #Leadership #Entrepreneurship

posts.topic: Building women up professionally and personally
posts.hook: You can't separate the professional woman from the whole woman
posts.caption:
You can't separate the professional woman from the whole woman

For a long time, the advice given to women in business was to keep the personal out of it.

Don't mention your kids. Don't talk about your health. Don't let them see you struggle. Be polished, be capable, be unbreakable.

I tried that for years. It was exhausting, and it often left me feeling more alone.

Here's what I believe now, after twenty years of leading teams and building communities of women:

You cannot build a woman up professionally without also building her up personally.

The woman negotiating a contract is the same woman who was up at 3am with a sick child. The woman pitching to a board is the same woman quietly managing a health scare. The woman launching a business is the same woman wondering if she's good enough.

When we only support the professional side, we miss most of what's actually holding women back.

So what does whole-woman support look like?

Mentoring that includes life, not just career. How do you manage guilt? How do you rest? How do you say no?

Celebrating personal wins, not just business milestones. Running a first 5km matters. Getting through a hard year matters.

Creating spaces where honesty is safe. Where a woman can say "I'm not okay" without it affecting how she's seen professionally.

Opening doors, not just giving advice. Introductions, referrals, recommendations. Advice is lovely. Opportunity is life-changing.

Being the woman you needed when you were starting out.

This is a big part of why I built The Giving Table. I wanted women to feel supported as whole people, with ambitions, doubts, families and lives beyond their work.

Because when you build up the whole woman, the professional success tends to follow.

Who's a woman who supported you as a person as well as in your career?

#WomenInBusiness #WomenSupportingWomen #Mentoring #Leadership #TheGivingTable

posts.topic: Giving as a business strategy
posts.hook: The three questions I ask before any business says yes to a cause
posts.caption:
The three questions I ask before any business says yes to a cause

Every week, I talk to business owners who want to "give back" but don't know where to start.

Some of them feel guilty they're not doing enough. Some have been burned by a partnership that felt more like a sales pitch. Some just don't know which of the hundred requests in their inbox deserves a yes.

After two decades of running charity events, both as a business giving and alongside charities asking for support, these are the three questions I always come back to.

1. Does this connect to who we actually are?

If you run a construction company and you sponsor a ballet gala because it looked glamorous, that's fine. But it won't stick. The giving that lasts is the giving that makes sense. Builders supporting housing charities. Hospitality supporting food rescue. Event people supporting events. When the cause matches your DNA, your team cares, your clients get it, and you stay.

2. Can we commit for three years, not three months?

Charities need people they can plan around. A smaller commitment you keep for years can do more good and build more trust than a big splash you can't sustain. I tell every business: give at a level you can repeat.

3. Are we willing to give time, not just money?

Money matters. I've spent my career raising it. But the businesses that get the most out of giving are often the ones whose people roll up their sleeves through volunteering days, pro bono expertise and time spent getting to know the cause.

That direct involvement can help people see the difference their work makes.

Here's what I've seen happen when businesses answer yes to all three:

Teams find a shared purpose. Relationships deepen. The business becomes known for its contribution as well as its product.

Over time, that can become part of how a business works and what it stands for.

If your business is giving right now, which of these three questions is the hardest one to answer honestly?

#CorporateGiving #CSR #Philanthropy #BusinessStrategy #CommunityImpact

posts.topic: How volunteering builds you and others
posts.hook: How volunteering builds the cause and the person
posts.caption:
How volunteering builds the cause and the person

When people talk about volunteering, they usually focus on what it gives the cause.

That matters enormously. I also want to talk about what volunteering gives the person who turns up.

Volunteering has built me.

Some of the most important skills I use every day in business, I learnt for free, wearing a lanyard, at events where I wasn't being paid a cent:

Calm under pressure. Nothing teaches you to think on your feet like a volunteer shift where the catering is late, the MC is missing and 400 guests are arriving in ten minutes.

Leading without authority. When you're coordinating volunteers, nobody has to listen to you. You learn to lead through respect, clarity and warmth. That's the best leadership training there is.

Empathy. Volunteering puts you face to face with people whose lives look very different from yours. It softens you in the best possible way.

Confidence. For women returning to work or changing careers, volunteering can be a place to rediscover what they're capable of.

Connections. Some of my most valuable relationships began side by side at a volunteer table. There's no pretence when you're both sorting raffle tickets.

And here's the beautiful part: none of this takes anything away from the cause. The charity gets your time and energy. You get growth, perspective and purpose. Nobody loses.

I can't think of anything else in life that works quite like that.

If you've been telling yourself you're too busy, or that you don't have anything to offer, I'd gently push back. You may have more to give, and more to gain, than you realise.

What's a skill you learnt through volunteering that you still use today?

#Volunteering #PersonalGrowth #Leadership #Community #WomenInBusiness

posts.topic: Building women up professionally and personally
posts.hook: The most powerful thing you can do for another woman costs nothing
posts.caption:
The most powerful thing you can do for another woman costs nothing

Say her name in rooms she isn't in.

Some of the biggest breaks of my career came from women who mentioned me when I wasn't there. A recommendation in a meeting. A name passed to a decision-maker. A quiet "you should talk to Liliana" over coffee.

I didn't know about most of them until years later. But they changed the course of my business.

Now I try to do the same, as often as I can. And I want to encourage every woman reading this to do it too.

Here's how to build women up when they're not watching:

Recommend her by name. Say what she does, why her work matters and who could benefit from knowing her.

Give credit precisely. When a woman's idea gets picked up in a meeting, say "that builds on what Sarah said earlier." Make sure it's attributed.

Share her work. A comment, a repost, a tag. On LinkedIn it takes seconds and increases her visibility more than you might think.

Put her forward for opportunities. Speaking slots, panels, awards or boards may be a good fit. Let her know about the opportunity and ask whether she'd like an introduction.

Defend her reputation. When someone criticises a woman unfairly, gently push back. Silence often reads as agreement.

I've watched too many talented women stay invisible because they were waiting to be noticed. Most opportunities don't come from being noticed. They come from being mentioned.

Supporting women can be practical, specific and often unseen.

Who is a woman whose work deserves more attention? Tag her in the comments and tell us why.

Let's say some names.

#WomenSupportingWomen #WomenInBusiness #Sponsorship #Leadership #Community

posts.topic: Questions to ask your keynote speakers
posts.hook: Five more speaker questions (the uncomfortable ones that save your event)
posts.caption:
Five more speaker questions (the uncomfortable ones that save your event)

The standard speaker brief is a good start. There are also a few less comfortable questions worth asking before you confirm a booking.

These questions can help prevent surprises for your audience, your team and your budget.

1. "Is there anything in your talk that could be sensitive for this audience?" Language, humour, personal stories, political references. What works at a corporate sales kick-off might not work at a charity luncheon. Better to know now.

2. "What's your cancellation policy, and do you have a backup plan?" Illness happens. Flights get cancelled. A professional speaker should be able to explain the arrangements clearly.

3. "Can we talk about fees, travel and inclusions in full?" Flights, accommodation, transfers, per diems, book sales, recording rights. I've seen budgets blow out over line items nobody discussed upfront.

4. "Are you happy for the session to be recorded or photographed?" Some speakers restrict this. If you're promising sponsors content from the day, you need to know.

5. "Can we have a briefing call a week out?" This is non-negotiable for me. It's where we align on the final audience, the introduction, the handover from the MC, and any last-minute changes. It's also where you get a real sense of who they are to work with.

And one question I ask myself: "Do this person's values align with ours?" The people we put on stage become part of the event's public identity.

Asking these questions helps everyone prepare properly. Clear expectations give the speaker and the organising team the best chance of delivering a good event.

What's the most awkward question you've ever had to ask a speaker? And was it worth it?

posts.topic: Relationships over sporadic connections
posts.hook: The simple system I use to keep relationships alive (when life is chaos)
posts.caption:
The simple system I use to keep relationships alive (when life is chaos)

Investing in relationships sounds lovely. But how do you actually do it when you're flat out?

Fair question. I run multiple businesses. I'm on the road a lot. My calendar is a work of fiction most weeks.

So here's the honest, unglamorous system I use.

1. I keep a short list. Not a CRM of thousands. A list of the 30 or so people I genuinely want in my life for the long term. Clients, collaborators, mentors, friends who happen to be in business.

2. I check in with no agenda. Every week, I reach out to two or three people on that list. No ask. Just "saw this and thought of you" or "how did that launch go?"

3. I write things down. When someone tells me their daughter is starting school or their mum is unwell, I make a note. Remembering details is one of the most powerful things you can do for a relationship.

4. I make introductions generously. The fastest way to deepen a relationship is to help someone else win. I'm always asking: who do I know that this person should meet?

5. I show up in person when it counts. Their launch. Their award night. Their charity event. A message is lovely; being in the room is unforgettable.

6. I'm honest when I've dropped the ball. Sometimes months go by. I don't pretend it didn't happen. "I've been terrible at staying in touch, and I've missed you" goes a long way.

None of this is complicated. It just requires intention and a bit of discipline.

Relationships are like gardens. They don't need constant attention, but they do need regular care. Neglect them for too long and something else grows in their place.

What's your system for staying connected with the people who matter? I'm always keen to steal a good idea.

#Relationships #Networking #Productivity #WomenInBusiness #Leadership

posts.topic: Questions to ask your MC before booking
posts.hook: Booking an MC for a charity event? These questions matter even more.
posts.caption:
Booking an MC for a charity event? These questions matter even more.

Charity events are a different beast. I've spent most of my career producing them, and the MC at a fundraiser carries a responsibility that goes well beyond keeping things on time.

They're helping a charity raise money it genuinely needs. They're often introducing people sharing deeply personal stories. And they need to make generous guests feel appreciated, not pressured.

So on top of the usual questions, here's what I ask an MC for a charity event:

1. "Do you have a connection to this cause, or are you willing to learn about it?" I want an MC to understand the mission and meet the team before stepping onto the stage.

2. "How would you introduce someone sharing a difficult personal story?" The introduction needs care and dignity. So does the response afterwards. Give the speaker space rather than rushing into a joke or the next item.

3. "How do you approach the fundraising moment?" Are they comfortable making the ask? Can they read when to push and when to pause? Have they worked alongside an auctioneer before?

4. "How will you acknowledge sponsors and donors?" Some supporters welcome public thanks. Others prefer to remain anonymous. The MC needs a clear brief on both.

5. "Do you offer a not-for-profit rate?" It's fine to ask respectfully, while recognising the preparation and professional work involved.

6. "What's your approach to humour in this room?" Humour is wonderful at charity events. Humour at the wrong moment can undo everything.

The right MC can make a real difference to the fundraising moment and the goodwill in the room.

Charity event organisers, what quality do you value most in an MC?

#CharityEvents #Fundraising #MC #NotForProfit #EventPlanning

posts.topic: Guide to lasting connections: first impressions to business deals
posts.hook: My guide to connections that last, Part 1: The first impression
posts.caption:
My guide to connections that last, Part 1: The first impression

People often ask how I've built such strong relationships over twenty years in business. Relationships that have led to partnerships, clients, friendships and millions raised for charity.

Over time, I've noticed a few habits that help. I'm sharing them in three parts, from the first meeting to working together.

Part 1 is where it all begins: the first meeting.

Be present. Put the phone away. Make eye contact. Listen to understand. Giving someone your full attention makes a difference.

Ask better questions. Swap "what do you do?" for "what are you most excited about at the moment?" or "what brought you here tonight?" Questions like these invite stories, and stories create connection.

Remember names and use them naturally. Repeat the name when you're introduced and use it once more in the conversation if it fits.

Find the human thread. A shared love of a cause, a hometown, kids the same age, a terrible first job. Business connections built on human common ground last far longer than those built on mutual usefulness.

Offer something before you ask for anything. An idea, an introduction, an encouraging word. Generosity in the first five minutes says more about you than any elevator pitch.

Leave warmly. Respect the other person's time and suggest a next step when it makes sense: "I'd love to introduce you to someone. May I email you tomorrow?"

A first impression isn't about impressing. It's about making the other person feel valued.

In Part 2, I'll share how I approach the follow-up and the slower work of staying in touch.

What's the most memorable first impression someone has made on you, and why did it stick?

#Networking #Relationships #FirstImpressions #WomenInBusiness #Connection

posts.topic: Guide to lasting connections: first impressions to business deals
posts.hook: My guide to connections that last, Part 2: The follow-up and the slow build
posts.caption:
My guide to connections that last, Part 2: The follow-up and the slow build

In Part 1, I talked about first impressions. Today: the part almost everyone gets wrong.

A promising first meeting can fade if nobody follows up, or if the first message feels like a sales pitch.

Here's how I turn a good first conversation into a lasting relationship.

Follow up within 48 hours where you can. Keep it personal: "It was lovely meeting you last night. I enjoyed hearing about your new venture." Mention something specific from the conversation.

Deliver on what you promised. If you said you'd make an introduction or send an article, do it. Quickly. Reliability is the foundation of trust, and it starts with small promises.

Don't pitch. Not yet. Maybe not for months. The fastest way to end a new connection is to treat it as a lead.

Stay on their radar with value. Comment thoughtfully on their posts. Share an opportunity you think suits them. Send a note when you see their business in the news.

Find a reason to meet again. Invite them to an event you think they'd enjoy. Suggest a coffee with no agenda. The second and third meetings are where relationships genuinely form.

Show up for their moments. Their launch, their award, their charity event. Being in the room for someone else's milestone says more than any message.

Be patient. Some relationships take years to turn into work together. Others remain valuable without ever becoming business.

The slow build feels inefficient. It isn't. It's the difference between a contact and a relationship.

In Part 3, I'll share how to have a business conversation while respecting the relationship.

What's your approach to following up after meeting someone new?

#Networking #Relationships #BusinessGrowth #FollowUp #WomenInBusiness

posts.topic: Guide to lasting connections: first impressions to business deals
posts.hook: My guide to connections that last, Part 3: From relationship to business deal
posts.caption:
My guide to connections that last, Part 3: From relationship to business deal

Welcome to the final part of my guide. We've covered first impressions and the slow build. Now, the question everyone secretly wants answered: how does a relationship become business?

Here's the truth: when you've done the first two parts well, the business part is usually the easiest.

Let the opportunity reveal itself. When you genuinely understand someone's goals and challenges, you'll naturally see where you can help. And because you've been generous for months, they'll often come to you first.

Ask permission to talk business. "I've got an idea that might help with what you mentioned. Would you be open to hearing it?" Give the other person a choice.

Be honest about fit. If you aren't the right person to help, say so and offer a useful referral if you can.

Make the proposal clear and leave room for a no. Explain the scope and price without pressure. The relationship matters whichever answer comes back.

Over-deliver on the first project. Your first piece of work together sets the tone for everything that follows. Treat it like an audition you're determined to ace.

Keep the relationship bigger than the transaction. Once the deal is done, keep showing up as you did before. Check in. Celebrate their wins. Don't disappear until the next invoice.

Say thank you, properly. A handwritten note, a thoughtful gift, a public acknowledgement. Gratitude turns a client into an advocate.

The best business deals I've ever done didn't feel like deals. They felt like a natural next step between two people who already trusted each other.

That's the whole guide: be present, build slowly, give generously, and let business grow from trust.

Which part of this three-part guide do you find hardest: the first meeting, staying in touch or the business conversation?

#BusinessDevelopment #Relationships #Sales #Networking #WomenInBusiness

posts.topic: Why rest and recharge matter
posts.hook: Rest isn't the reward for finishing. It's the fuel for starting.
posts.caption:
Rest isn't the reward for finishing. It's the fuel for starting.

The events industry has a badge-of-honour culture around exhaustion.

We swap stories about 20-hour bump-in days. We joke about living on cold coffee and adrenaline. We wear our tiredness like a medal, because it proves how hard we work.

I did it for years. I was proud of it.

I'm not anymore.

Here's what I've learnt after more than twenty years and thousands of events: rest is not something you earn once the work is done. In business, the work is never done. If you wait until it is, you'll never rest at all.

Rest is what makes good work possible.

When I'm properly rested:

I make better decisions, faster.

I'm more patient with my team and kinder to my clients.

I spot problems before they become crises.

I have space for creative ideas, rather than just reacting to my inbox.

I enjoy the work I love, instead of just surviving it.

When I'm exhausted, decisions and mistakes can take longer to work through. Rest helps me return with a clearer head.

The hardest part was believing I was allowed to stop. Many women juggle a business, family and other people's needs, then feel guilty taking time for themselves.

So let me say it clearly, in case you need to hear it today: you are allowed to rest. Not because you've finished. Because you're human.

Your business needs you for the long haul. Not just for this week.

How do you truly recharge? I'm genuinely curious what works for different people.

#Rest #Wellbeing #Burnout #WomenInBusiness #EventIndustry

posts.topic: Learning from people who've done the work
posts.hook: Learn from the people with dirt under their fingernails
posts.caption:
Learn from the people with dirt under their fingernails

There's never been more business advice available than right now.

Courses. Podcasts. Frameworks. Ten-step formulas. Coaches who've coached coaches who've coached coaches.

Some of it is brilliant. A lot of it is theory dressed up as experience.

After more than twenty years in business, I want to learn from people who have done the work and lived with the consequences of their decisions.

Why does it matter so much?

Because theory skips the messy middle. A framework will tell you how to grow a business. Someone who's done it will tell you about the month they couldn't make payroll, the client who nearly broke them, and what they'd do differently.

Because practitioners know what actually matters. When I'm planning an event, the best advice rarely comes from a textbook. It comes from the stage manager who's done 500 shows, or the caterer who knows exactly how long it takes to serve 800 guests.

Because real experience includes failure. People who've done the work have made the mistakes. Their advice is shaped by scar tissue, not just success.

Because they understand context. Useful advice often starts with "it depends," followed by a clear explanation of what matters in your situation.

This is one of the founding principles of The Giving Table. Every speaker and masterclass host we bring in has done the work themselves. Built the business. Raised the money. Led the team. Survived the hard years.

Theory has its place. But when you're making real decisions with real consequences, learn from someone who's been there.

Who's someone who's actually done the work that you've learnt the most from?

#Mentoring #Leadership #BusinessAdvice #WomenInBusiness #TheGivingTable

posts.topic: Showing up when you don't feel like it
posts.hook: Consistency is the most underrated success strategy in business
posts.caption:
Consistency is the most underrated success strategy in business

Everyone wants the big break. The viral moment. The game-changing deal.

After more than 2,500 events and two decades in business, I can tell you that almost none of my success came from a single big moment.

It came from showing up. Again, and again, and again.

Turning up to the industry breakfast when I was tired. Sending the follow-up email when it felt pointless. Posting my insights when nobody was engaging. Going back to the charity committee year after year. Doing the work properly even when nobody would notice if I cut corners.

None of it felt like progress at the time. All of it added up.

Here's why I believe consistency beats talent, luck and even brilliance:

It builds trust. People learn what they can expect from you. Reliability gives them confidence to work with you and recommend you.

It compounds. One coffee meeting does little. Fifty over a few years builds a network. One post does little. Two hundred builds a reputation.

It outlasts motivation. Motivation comes and goes. Habits stay. The people who succeed long-term aren't the most motivated. They're the most consistent.

It separates you from the crowd. Most people give up quietly when results don't come fast enough. Simply staying in the game puts you ahead.

When I founded The Giving Table, I knew one great event wouldn't build a community. Showing up month after month would. That's still the plan.

If progress feels slow, look at what's worth continuing and what needs adjusting. Consistency works best when you're paying attention to what you're learning.

The people who make it aren't always the ones who started strongest. They're the ones who kept showing up.

What's one thing you've stayed consistent with that's paid off over time?

#Consistency #Success #Entrepreneurship #WomenInBusiness #Leadership

posts.topic: Showing up when you don't feel like it
posts.hook: The days you least want to show up are the days that count most
posts.caption:
The days you least want to show up are the days that count most

I'll let you in on a secret: I don't always feel like showing up.

There have been mornings I've sat in the car outside a venue, coffee in hand, wondering if I had anything left to give. Days after a disappointment, a loss, a sleepless night, a hard conversation. Days I'd have given almost anything to stay home.

And almost every time, I walked in anyway.

Not because I'm superhuman. Because I've learnt something over twenty years that I wish I'd known at the start:

Small, reliable actions can matter most during a difficult week.

The clients I've kept for a decade remember the day I turned up for them during my own tough week. The charities I've supported remember who was there on the rainy night when half the guest list cancelled. My team remembers how I behaved when things were falling apart, not when everything was going well.

Reputation isn't built on your best days. It's built on your hardest ones.

Here's what helps me show up when I don't feel like it:

I remember who's counting on me. It's rarely about me. There's a client, a team, a cause, a family on the other side of my effort.

I lower the bar for how I feel, not for what I deliver. I don't need to feel inspired. I just need to be there and do the next thing well.

I start small. Five minutes. One call. One task. Momentum usually follows.

I'm honest when I need to be. Showing up doesn't mean pretending. Sometimes it means saying "I'm having a tough day, but I'm here."

Showing up isn't about perfection. It's about presence.

And on the days you need to stop, rest or ask for help. Looking after yourself matters too.

What gets you through the door on the days you'd rather not?

#Resilience #Leadership #Consistency #WomenInBusiness #Mindset

posts.topic: Learning from people who've done the work
posts.hook: How to tell if someone has actually done the work (before you take their advice)
posts.caption:
How to tell if someone has actually done the work (before you take their advice)

How can you tell whether someone's advice comes from practical experience?

It's not always obvious. Here are the signals I look for before taking someone's advice or inviting them to speak to our community.

They talk about specifics, not just principles. Real experience comes with real details. Numbers, timelines, names of places, the exact moment it went wrong. Theory stays vague.

They share failures freely. People who've done the work aren't afraid to tell you what didn't work. If someone only has success stories, I get curious about what they're leaving out.

They say "it depends." Experienced people know context matters. Beware anyone with a single formula that works for everyone.

Their results are visible. A business you can see. A track record you can check. Clients or colleagues who'll speak about their work.

Their experience is relevant to today's conditions. Industries change, so I ask how they keep their knowledge current.

Other practitioners respect them. The best test of all: what do people in the same field say about them when they're not in the room?

None of this means theory is worthless. Some of the most brilliant thinkers I know have never run a business. But I want to know which one I'm listening to, so I can weigh the advice accordingly.

I hold myself to this standard too. My lessons come from more than 2,500 events, 20-plus years in business and over $70 million raised for charity, including the mistakes along the way. If I haven't done something, I'll tell you.

That's the kind of honesty I think we all deserve from the people we learn from.

What signals do you look for before trusting someone's advice?

#Leadership #CriticalThinking #Mentoring #BusinessGrowth #WomenInBusiness
